sources.news_title: Katie Zacharia under investigation by California State Bar over claiming to be lawyer
sources.text:
Katie Zacharia under investigation by California State Bar over claiming to be lawyer
A spokesperson for Zacharia said the investigation is "politically motivated and a clear waste of the State Bar’s time and resources."
The California State Bar has placed Katie Zacharia under investigation after a watchdog group filed a complaint, claiming that she violated the law after claiming to be a lawyer. This comes after Zacharia served for a brief stint as White House Press Secretary.
During that same time period, reporting was highlighted that showed she never passed the bar exam, but has claimed to be a lawyer. The group, Campaign for Accountability (CfA), wrote in a letter claiming that she broke the law in California.
“Ms. Zacharia has represented herself as a lawyer repeatedly to buttress her reputation and credibility as a television legal commentator and now as the White House spokesperson, yet it seems it was all a lie,” CfA executive director Michelle said about the letter in a release.
The complaint requested that "the State Bar of California investigate whether Katie S. Zacharia violated sections 6125 and 6126 of the California Business and Professions Code."
The California law states that those that those "advertising or holding himself or herself out as practicing or entitled to practice law or otherwise practicing law who is not an active licensee of the State Bar, or otherwise authorized pursuant to statute or court rule to practice law in this state at the time of doing so, is guilty of a misdemeanor punishable by up to one year in a county jail or by a fine of up to one thousand dollars ($1,000), or by both that fine and imprisonment."
The state bar responded earlier this month and confirmed that they placed Zacharia under investigation. In a statement to the LA Times, Zacharia's spokesperson said that the complaint was "baseless" and is "politically motivated and a clear waste of the State Bar’s time and resources. We are confident it will be dismissed with no finding of wrongdoing."
Zacharia has maintained that she was able to have the title of lawyer as she was not required to pass the bar exam for her later legal work in China.
She told Human Events Daily host Jack Posobiec in an interview in October. "After moving to China, I think I didn't really think much of the bar results or consider that something that I needed to focus on. And I was offered a job in an international practice division of a Chinese law firm called Zhong Lun Law Firm."
She added at the time, "I consulted for a very long time many people in the field, is it okay and acceptable if I label myself lawyer, not attorney at law, not Katie Zachariah Esquire, but lawyer, and provide legal analysis, not legal advice? And they said absolutely, absolutely across the board. You can call yourself a lawyer.”
According to Russell and Hill and other sources, there is a distinction between lawyer and attorney. Lawyer means that someone has a law degree while an attorney is licensed in a specific location to practice law after passing the bar exam.

sources.news_title: Trump's fired spokesperson lashes out as state bar probes her 'lawyer' claims: report
sources.text:
Problems continue to follow President Donald Trump's last press secretary, who was fired in less than a week, as she faces a state bar investigation.
According to Saturday reports, the State Bar of California is investigating Katie Zacharia over allegations that she passed herself off as a lawyer without ever earning a law license. Zacharia lasted just five days as White House press secretary and also offered legal analysis as a commentator on Newsmax.
Zacharia graduated from Pepperdine University's law school in 2011, but she never passed the bar exam in California or anywhere else in the country, reporters discovered shortly after she started as White House press secretary. Before joining the administration, she routinely presented herself as a lawyer during cable news appearances, and her LinkedIn profile listed a stint as a general counsel for a California nonprofit, according to reporting by The Guardian.
Shortly after her first White House press conference, Zacharia was asked by a reporter where she took the bar exam, and she said, "in China."
The probe she now faces stems from a complaint the watchdog group Campaign for Accountability lodged with the California bar in mid-October, according to reporting by The Washington Post. The bar later notified the organization that it had put an investigator and a legal adviser on the case, per The Guardian, and The Post noted that bar officials confirmed the investigation in a letter to the group on Thursday.
In its complaint, the Campaign for Accountability warned that in California, falsely claiming to be a lawyer "isn't puffery; it's a crime."
"Zacharia may have thought she was just playing a lawyer on TV, but by repeatedly holding herself out as an attorney on news programs, she was pretending to have authority she lacks," Michelle Kuppersmith, the director of the Campaign for Accountability, wrote in a public statement. "We're pleased the California bar is taking this matter seriously and investigating."
In a post on X, Zacharia called the Campaign for Accountability "a radical leftist group founded by CREW alumni, incubated by the Arabella network, and bankrolled by George Soros' Open Society."

Ex-Trump press secretary Katie Zacharia under probe for posing as lawyer without passing bar
sources.text:
Former White House press secretary Katie Zacharia is facing an investigation by the State Bar of California over allegations that she presented herself as a qualified lawyer despite never passing a bar examination in the United States.
The investigation follows a complaint filed in October by Campaign for Accountability, a non-profit watchdog organisation. The California bar informed the group earlier this month that an investigator and legal adviser had been assigned to examine the allegations.
Before joining the Trump administration, Zacharia appeared on several television programmes and described herself as a lawyer. Her LinkedIn profile also listed her as the general counsel of a California-based non-profit organisation. Trump referred to her as an “attorney” when announcing her appointment as White House press secretary.
Although Zacharia graduated from Pepperdine University with a law degree in 2011, she has not passed the bar examination in California or any other US state, according to The Guardian.
Michelle Kuppersmith, director of Campaign for Accountability, questioned Zacharia's repeated claims about her professional credentials.
“Zacharia may have thought she was just playing a lawyer on TV, but by repeatedly holding herself out as an attorney on news programs, she was pretending to have authority she lacks,” Kuppersmith said.
“We’re pleased the California bar is taking this matter seriously and investigating,” she added.
Zacharia has rejected the allegations. A spokesperson for her told The Guardian: “These are baseless allegations. This complaint is politically motivated and a clear waste of the state bar’s time and resources. We are confident it will be dismissed with no finding of wrongdoing.”
Zacharia had earlier defended her use of the term “lawyer”, arguing that it was distinct from “attorney”, which she said referred to someone licensed to practise law. In an email to the newspaper, she cited an American Bar Association Journal article discussing the distinction between the two terms.
A spokesperson for the State Bar of California confirmed that it was aware of reports concerning Zacharia, describing her as a non-licensee. However, the spokesperson stressed that an investigation or complaint does not establish that someone has engaged in the unauthorised practice of law or violated state statutes. The bar also said its investigations remain confidential.
Campaign for Accountability had urged the regulator to examine whether Zacharia misrepresented her qualifications to the public and determine whether she violated California law.
The controversy follows Zacharia's brief tenure as Trump's press secretary. She replaced Karoline Leavitt in mid-October but left the position after five days, making her the shortest-serving person to hold the role. During her first press briefing, she stumbled over some of her remarks and took questions primarily from conservative media outlets.

sources.news_title: Former White House press secretary faces investigation
sources.text:
(The Center Square) – The State Bar of California has opened an investigation into former White House Press Secretary Katie Zacharia over allegations that she unlawfully misrepresented herself as a licensed attorney.
The investigation adds to the scrutiny surrounding Zacharia's legal credentials following her brief tenure in the White House. She stepped down as press secretary on Oct. 16 after just five days on the job.
The state bar's inquiry follows a formal complaint filed by the watchdog group Campaign for Accountability. Investigators are reviewing claims that Zacharia repeatedly referred to herself as a lawyer — and appeared under that title on Fox News, CNN and various podcasts — despite never passing a bar exam after earning her law degree in 2011 from Pepperdine University in Malibu.
According to the complaint, Zacharia also listed titles including "outside counsel" and "General Counsel" on her resume and LinkedIn profile.
Under California law, falsely advertising or holding oneself out as entitled to practice law without an active license is a misdemeanor. A conviction carries penalties of up to one year in county jail and a $1,000 fine.
“Zacharia may have thought she was just playing a lawyer on TV, but by repeatedly holding herself out as an attorney on news programs, she was pretending to have authority she lacks,” said Michelle Kuppersmith, executive director of Campaign for Accountability.
“We’re pleased the California Bar is taking this matter seriously and investigating," Kuppersmith said in a press release.
The Center Square reached out to Campaign for Accountability for comment, but did not receive a response by publication time
The Center Square's attempts to reach Zacharia for an interview or comments were also unsuccessful. However, a spokesperson for Zacharia dismissed the complaint as politically motivated and a waste of resources.
Zacharia previously acknowledged that she failed the California bar exam, attributing the result to distractions from a recent marriage and an impending move to Beijing. She has maintained that she worked in international transactional law in China and stated that unnamed legal experts advised her she was permitted to use the title of "lawyer" while providing media commentary.
Before joining the administration, Zacharia worked as a senior communications adviser for Trump Media & Technology Group, the parent company of Truth Social.

sources.news_title: Ex-Press Sec Katie Zacharia Faces California Bar Investigation Over Claims She Was a Lawyer
sources.text:
Trump's Fired Press Sec Katie Zacharia Faces California Bar Investigation Over Claims She Was a Lawyer — Following Her Five-Day White House Stint
Nov. 20 2026, Published 6:53 p.m. ET
The State Bar of California is investigating allegations that former White House press secretary Katie Zacharia misrepresented herself as a lawyer despite never passing a bar exam, RadarOnline.com can reveal.
The inquiry follows an October complaint from Campaign for Accountability, a nonprofit watchdog group. The bar told the organization that the complaint had been forwarded for further investigation and assigned to an investigator and legal adviser. The inquiry is ongoing, and no finding of wrongdoing has been made.
Watchdog Complaint Raises Questions About Lawyer Title
Zacharia's spokesperson called the allegations "baseless" and described the complaint as politically motivated. The spokesperson said they expect it to be dismissed.
Campaign for Accountability alleges Zacharia repeatedly identified herself as a lawyer during television appearances and on other platforms. The complaint cites an appearance on The Greg Kelly Show in which she reportedly said, "I'm a lawyer," as well as news broadcasts that identified her as one.
The group also pointed to a past LinkedIn profile describing Zacharia as general counsel for the California nonprofit Fix California. It questioned claims about her work with the World Bank and International Finance Corp.
Executive Director Michelle Kuppersmith welcomed the bar's decision to investigate, saying Zacharia had presented herself as having professional authority she did not hold.
Katie Zacharia Says She Was Advised She Could Use The Term
Zacharia graduated from Pepperdine University School of Law in 2011 but has not been licensed to practice law in California or another U.S. state, according to the complaint.
She has said she took the bar exam after law school but did not pass. In comments to USA Today, Zacharia said she did not retake it before moving to China with her husband, where she worked with an international-practice team at a Chinese law firm.
She has also argued that "lawyer" and “attorney” are distinct terms, saying legal experts told her she could describe herself as a lawyer because she held a law degree. The distinction is central to the complaint and the state bar's review.
California Law Limits Claims of Legal Authority
California law makes it a misdemeanor for someone who is not an active licensee to hold themselves out as entitled to practice law. Potential penalties include up to one year in county jail, a fine of up to $1,000, or both.
Campaign for Accountability has asked the state bar to examine whether Zacharia's public statements and professional descriptions violated the law. The group also asked that any possible violations be referred to prosecutors.
The bar’s decision to investigate does not mean Zacharia broke the law or that criminal charges have been filed. Her spokesperson said the complaint would be dismissed without a finding of wrongdoing.
Inquiry Follows Brief White House Tenure
Zacharia’s professional background drew scrutiny after President Donald Trump named her press secretary in October. She held the role for five days, making her the shortest-serving person in the position, before leaving the White House.
Trump had called Zacharia an attorney when announcing her appointment. During the ensuing controversy, he said her legal credentials were not a requirement for the press secretary job.
The California State Bar has not announced a conclusion in the case. Its investigation will determine whether the allegations warrant further action.

sources.news_title: Ex-Trump Press Secretary Katie Zacharia Faces Lawyer Claims Probe
sources.text:
Former White House press secretary Katie Zacharia is being investigated by the State Bar of California after a watchdog group alleged that she repeatedly presented herself as a lawyer despite apparently never being licensed to practice law.
The Campaign for Accountability (CfA) said Thursday that it had received a letter from the California Bar confirming that an investigation was opened after the group filed a complaint against Zacharia on October 14.
The complaint claims Zacharia may have breached California law by repeatedly identifying herself as an attorney during appearances on television news programs.
CfA said published reports suggest Zacharia has never been admitted to practice law in California or in any other US jurisdiction.
In a letter received on November 19, the California Bar told CfA that the complaint had been assigned to an investigator and legal adviser for review.
The organization was also told that it would receive notice of the outcome once the inquiry was complete.
Michelle Kuppersmith, executive director of the Campaign for Accountability, said the group welcomed the Bar’s decision to examine the allegations.
‘Zacharia may have thought she was simply playing a lawyer on television, but by repeatedly presenting herself as an attorney on news programs, she was claiming authority she does not possess,’ Kuppersmith said.
The complaint claims Zacharia may have violated California law by repeatedly identifying herself as an attorney during television appearances
President Donald Trump initially appeared surprised when reporters questioned Zacharia’s legal background after describing her as an ‘attorney’ while announcing her appointment
During a Fox News appearance on August 31, 2026, Zacharia discussed the Charlie Kirk murder case and said, ‘As a lawyer, the procedural steps are absolutely critical to ensure that they get this right’
‘We are pleased that the California Bar is treating this matter seriously and conducting an investigation.’
Before joining the White House, Zacharia served as a senior communications adviser at the parent company of President Donald Trump’s media platform, Truth Social. She had earlier worked as a Department of Homeland Security spokesperson under Kristi Noem.
She was also a familiar presence on Fox News and Newsmax, where she appeared as a political and legal commentator.
Zacharia appeared on CNN and One America News as well, discussing legal and political matters while being identified in television graphics as an attorney.
During a Fox News appearance on August 31, 2026, she addressed the Charlie Kirk murder case, saying, ‘As a lawyer, the procedural steps are absolutely critical to ensure that they get this right.’
The controversy intensified when Zacharia was asked directly where she had passed the bar exam, which is required to become a licensed attorney.
As Trump left the White House with reporters following her first and only briefing, one journalist challenged his description of Zacharia as an attorney and asked which state had issued her license.
Trump directed the question to his press secretary, who replied, ‘When I moved to China,’ without providing any further explanation.
The exchange prompted additional scrutiny of her credentials, particularly after reports indicated that Zacharia’s name did not appear in the attorney directories for any US state or territory.
During her brief tenure as press secretary, Zacharia acknowledged that she was not a licensed attorney. She said she failed her first bar examination after graduating from Pepperdine Law School in 2011.
She explained that she had been ‘distracted’ and ‘overwhelmed’ while preparing to move to China with her then-husband.
Zacharia subsequently joined Zhong Lun, one of China’s largest law firms.
She spent nearly two years as an associate on the firm’s international practice team and later said she worked on multimillion-dollar shareholder agreements and cross-border transactions.
Zacharia has argued that her law degree provided the credentials needed for that work, even though she never passed a US bar examination.
After returning to the United States, she did not take the exam again. She said she had four children in six years and had never planned to practice law.
Trump initially appeared caught off guard by questions about Zacharia’s legal credentials after referring to her as an ‘attorney’ in his announcement appointing her.
When reporters asked which state she had passed the bar exam in, Trump turned to Zacharia and repeated, ‘Which state?’
As scrutiny grew, Trump continued to defend her. He said he ‘wasn’t hiring her to be a lawyer,’ praised her loyalty and accused the media of treating her ‘very unfairly.’
Before Zacharia resigned on October 16, Trump said he had asked her, ‘Is this for you?’ He added that he told her he would reconsider the position if he were in her place.
A week after she left the role, Trump said Zacharia had ‘freaked out’ amid the pressure and intense media attention surrounding the job.
The investigation does not establish that Zacharia broke any law, and the allegations have not been proven.
The California Bar has not reported any findings or announced disciplinary action against Zacharia. The inquiry will determine whether the allegations justify further proceedings.

sources.text:
Trump's Former Press Secretary Katie Zacharia Faces California Bar Investigation Over Claim of Practicing Law Without a License
Her reported nonprofit legal role and television appearances are central to a watchdog complaint
Katie Zacharia is facing a California State Bar investigation into allegations that she repeatedly presented herself as a lawyer despite never being admitted to practise in the United States. The inquiry centres on her television appearances and reported legal roles.
Campaign for Accountability filed its complaint on 14 October 2026. In a letter dated 6 November, the State Bar said it was assigning the complaint to an investigator and legal adviser. The watchdog announced the letter on 19 November. The assignment confirms that the allegations are being examined, not that misconduct has been established.
Television Appearances Feature in the Complaint
Zacharia graduated from Pepperdine University's law school in 2011 but did not pass the California bar examination. She has acknowledged failing the exam and not retaking it. Licensing records cited in the complaint have not identified an admission to practise in another US jurisdiction.
The watchdog cited an October 5 appearance on The Greg Kelly Show, during which Zacharia described herself as a lawyer. It also said she had been identified as a legal professional in at least 18 Fox News appearances since March 2025. These examples underpin its allegation that she repeatedly represented herself as having professional status she did not hold.
The complaint also questions claims that Zacharia served as outside counsel to the World Bank and the International Finance Corporation. These remain allegations, not established findings about her work for either institution.
Fix California Role Raises Questions About Her Responsibilities
Another issue is Zacharia's reported role as general counsel for Fix California, a nonprofit founded by Richard Grenell. Her professional profile listed the position as full-time employment from January 2024 to March 2025.
The complaint asks the State Bar to examine whether her responsibilities involved legal advice or work requiring a licence. The title of general counsel does not, by itself, establish unauthorised practice; the duties she performed would be relevant.
Zacharia has defended describing herself as a lawyer. She said legal professionals advised that the description was appropriate because she held a law degree. She has maintained that she provided legal analysis rather than legal advice. Her representative called the allegations politically motivated, said no laws had been violated, and expressed confidence the inquiry would find no wrongdoing.
Zacharia left her White House press secretary position on 16 October, after five days. The complaint was filed two days earlier, but no connection between her departure and the investigation has been established.
What California Law Says About Unlicensed Practice
California Business and Professions Code Section 6125 prohibits practising law in the state without an active State Bar licence. Section 6126(a) makes it a misdemeanour to practise law, or to advertise or hold oneself out as practising or entitled to practise law, without authorisation.
A violation can carry up to one year in county jail, a fine of up to $1,000 (£760), or both. These are statutory penalties, not charges or sentences imposed on Zacharia.
Campaign for Accountability has asked the State Bar to refer any substantiated violations to the Ventura County District Attorney or another appropriate prosecutor. The regulator has confirmed only that the complaint was assigned for investigation. No finding has been announced, and Zacharia denies wrongdoing.

Katie Zacharia’s Legal Credentials Come Under Scrutiny
Zacharia graduated from Pepperdine University School of Law in 2011, but she has not been admitted to practice law in California or any other U.S. jurisdiction, according to the watchdog’s complaint. The organization alleges that she repeatedly described herself as a lawyer during television appearances and podcasts. Its complaint points to an October 5 appearance on “The Greg Kelly Show,” during which Zacharia reportedly stated, “I’m a lawyer.”
It also identifies at least 18 Fox News appearances in which she was described on screen as a lawyer. Beyond her television work, the watchdog raised questions about claims that she served as outside counsel to the World Bank and the International Finance Corporation. The complaint also highlighted her previous LinkedIn description of herself as general counsel for Fix California, a nonprofit organization.
According to the Los Angeles Times, Zacharia acknowledged that she did not pass the California bar exam after graduating from law school. She explained that she was preparing to move to China with her husband at the time and did not expect to need a California license while living abroad. The distinction between obtaining a law degree and being licensed to practice law is central to the investigation.
Katie Zacharia Could Face Penalties If Violations Are Established
California law restricts individuals who are not licensed attorneys from representing themselves as authorized to practice law. Under Section 6126 of the California Business and Professions Code, a person who unlawfully holds themselves out as entitled to practice law can face misdemeanor penalties. Those penalties can include up to one year in county jail, a fine of up to $1,000, or both.
Campaign for Accountability has asked the State Bar to examine whether Zacharia’s statements and previous professional roles violated those restrictions. The watchdog also requested that any potential violations be referred to the appropriate prosecutors. However, opening an investigation does not mean criminal charges have been filed.
The State Bar told Newsweek that neither receiving a complaint nor investigating one establishes that unauthorized legal practice occurred. Zacharia has not been convicted of any offense related to the allegations, and her spokesperson maintains that the complaint will ultimately be dismissed.
Katie Zacharia’s Brief White House Tenure Draws Fresh Attention
The investigation comes roughly a month after Zacharia’s unusually short tenure as Trump’s White House press secretary. She took over the position in October but remained in the role for only a few days. Questions about her legal qualifications became a prominent issue during that period, particularly after she was asked where she had passed the bar exam.
Zacharia initially responded by referring to her move to China, where she previously worked at an international law firm. Her answer prompted additional scrutiny because obtaining a law degree does not automatically qualify someone to practice law in California. Trump subsequently addressed the controversy, telling reporters that her legal credentials were not a requirement for the press secretary position.
“Well, I wasn’t hiring her to be a lawyer,” the president said, according to Newsweek.
He also defended her loyalty, saying she had supported him for a long time. Zacharia left the White House role in mid-October, but the complaint concerning her professional credentials remained active. The California State Bar’s decision to investigate now places those allegations under formal review, with the outcome yet to be determined.

sources.news_title: California State Bar opens investigation into former White House press secretary Katie Zacharia
sources.text:
LOS ANGELES — The State Bar of California has opened an investigation into Katie Zacharia who faced scrutiny during her brief stint as White House press secretary for calling herself a lawyer despite never passing a bar exam.
The probe, which was made public on Thursday, comes in response to a complaint submitted last month by the nonprofit watchdog Campaign for Accountability alleging that Zacharia may have violated California law by touting herself as lawyer.
While Zacharia, a Huntington Beach, California, native, received a law degree from Pepperdine University in 2011, she did not pass the bar exam in California or any other state. Yet, since at least early 2025 she has described herself as a lawyer on national television and in podcasts, including on "The Greg Kelly Show" and CNN, and has been identified on screen as a lawyer in at least 18 appearances on Fox News, according to the complaint.
"Ms. Zacharia has represented herself as a lawyer repeatedly to buttress her reputation and credibility as a television legal commentator and now as the White House spokesperson, yet it seems it was all a lie. In California, calling yourself a lawyer without a license isn't puffery; it's a crime," the organization's executive director Michelle Kuppersmith said in a news release last month.
The watchdog's complaint alleges Zacharia claimed to have served as "outside counsel" to the World Bank and the International Finance Corporation, and previously listed herself on LinkedIn as full-time General Counsel of Fix California, a nonprofit.
A spokesperson for Zacharia denied that she had violated any laws in a text message to the Los Angeles Times, calling the accusations "baseless."
"This complaint is politically motivated and a clear waste of the State Bar's time and resources. We are confident it will be dismissed with no finding of wrongdoing," the spokesperson said.
Under California state law a person presenting themselves as being entitled to practice law without an active state bar license could be charged with a misdemeanor and face up to a year in county jail and a $1,000 fine.
Zacharia addressed the scrutiny last month in an interview with conservative outlet Human Events, saying she had been preparing to take the bar exam in California shortly after getting married and was busy preparing for a move to China to join her new husband, who had been working in private equity in Beijing.
"I was obviously incredibly distracted and overwhelmed and excited for finally being married to someone who I'd been long distance from for at least a year," Zacharia told the outlet, adding that the results of the exam were "somewhat inconsequential" because she knew she would not need the credential in China.
She said she had consulted several legal experts to ensure the title of lawyer was accurate when offering legal analysis and "they said absolutely, absolutely across the board. You can call yourself a lawyer," she told the outlet.
Zacharia added that it was "unfortunate that people dub this as some kind of conspiracy."
(Times staff writer Clara Harter contributed to this report.)

sources.news_title: Katie Zacharia now faces probe over her repeated claims to be a lawyer
Trump Ex–Press Secretary’s Claim to Be Lawyer Comes Back to Bite Her
sources.text:
Trump Ex–Press Secretary’s Claim to Be Lawyer Comes Back to Bite Her
The State Bar of California has opened an investigation into Katie Zacharia.
Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images
Katie Zacharia was the White House press secretary for just five days, but her brief tenure has already come back to haunt her.
The State Bar of California has opened an investigation into the 42-year-old and her self-purported legal expertise, Popular Info reported Thursday.
Prior to joining the Trump administration, Zacharia made a career for herself as an on-air commentator by claiming to be a lawyer. This included multiple appearances on Fox News and Newsmax, where her chyrons framed her as something of a legal expert.
But she was not. Last month, Popular Info first reported that Zacharia was not actually licensed to practice law anywhere in the country. She obtained her J.D. from Pepperdine Caruso Law in 2011, according to her LinkedIn profile. Her work history also includes a gig as “general counsel” for a Ric Grenell–operated nonprofit based in California, though Popular Info’s Judd Legum found she held no credentials to practice law there.
Zacharia is not listed as a member of the bar in Texas or Washington, D.C., either, despite evidence that she also worked in both places in a legal capacity. She told reporters after her single press briefing that she took the bar “when [she] moved to China,” but that is impossible under Chinese law. Zacharia eventually admitted she never passed the bar but thought that referring to herself as a “lawyer” instead of an “attorney” clarified her lack of credentials.
Public backlash to the revelations—and her lackluster performance as press secretary—quickly pushed her out of the White House.
The California investigation is the result of an October 14 complaint filed by the Campaign for Accountability, a nonprofit watchdog group based in Washington. At the time, the organization asked the California State Bar to examine whether Zacharia had violated state law when she functioned as general counsel. Now it seems they’ll get some answers.
“Zacharia may have thought she was just playing a lawyer on TV, but by repeatedly holding herself out as an attorney on news programs, she was pretending to have authority she lacks,” CFA executive director Michelle Kuppersmith said in a statement. “We’re pleased the California Bar is taking this matter seriously and investigating.”
Why the Heck Is Kyrsten Sinema at the Senate Right Now?
The former senator is trying to get her ex-colleagues to support a dangerous bill.
Former Senator Kyrsten Sinema
Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images
Former Senator Kyrsten Sinema
Former Arizona Senator Kyrsten Sinema is back on Capitol Hill urging her former colleagues to support a dangerous permitting reform bill, The Washington Sun reported Thursday.
The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, or BAAJA, would fast-track approvals for the construction of energy, mining, and infrastructure projects by severely limiting environmental challenges, radically altering transmission approvals, and even allowing the fossil fuel companies to sue the government if they can show they were discriminated against based on fuel type. The bill has been fiercely opposed by environmental groups and tribal organizations.
Sinema is not a registered lobbyist, but she co-chairs the Artificial Intelligence Infrastructure Coalition, a group of tech companies advocating on behalf of energy-hungry data centers. A spokesperson for the group told the Sun that Sinema was “not doing any work on behalf of us.”
A spokesperson for Sinema told the Sun that Sinema had stepped in at the request of her former colleagues.
“She is not helping on behalf of any person, and has no client or compensation here. She cares about her friends and is happy to help,” the spokesperson said.
Dylan Hedtler-Gaudette, the Project on Government Oversight’s director of government affairs, raised concerns about Sinema’s involvement.
“Maybe she’s just passionate about permitting reform, but I would suspect that’s not what’s happening,” Hedtler-Gaudette told the Sun. “She probably has a vested interest in this bill for a client or someone else.”
Before this, Sinema was most known for her “independent” heel turn, voting against workers’ rights and health care advances after campaigning as a next-generation progressive. More recently, she was sued under a North Carolina law for “home-wrecking” her bodyguard’s marriage.
Todd Blanche’s Wife Abruptly Yanks Shady Supplements Off Website
Kristine Blanche removed some of the products on her supplement-selling website, which claimed to treat illnesses with no FDA-approved cure, after a reporter reached out.
Kristine Blanche attends the confirmation hearing for her husband, Attorney General Todd Blanche, in July.
Photo by Win McNamee/Getty Images
Kristine Blanche attends the confirmation hearing for her husband, Attorney General Todd Blanche, in July.
Attorney General Todd Blanche’s wife, Kristine, was appointed in April to an advisory board for the National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health and tasked with supporting research on alternative medicines. But as it turns out, she was profiting from unproven supplements and treatments all along.
A Guardian investigation published Thursday revealed that Kristine Blanche has been selling herbal compounds on a page of her website titled “Dr Blanche’s Dispensary.” Some of Blanche’s tinctures claim to help people recover from Epstein-Barr virus, more commonly known as mono, though she misspelled the name of the disease as “Epstien.” There are no Food and Drug Administration–approved medications that treat the disease.
Other listings on the page claim to treat human papillomavirus, or HPV, though those run about $63 a bottle through Blanche’s website. Another one of Blanche’s offerings purports to “boost” men’s testosterone for a measly $595 a pop.
As a member of the health board, Kristine Blanche oversees a $170 million annual budget.
Blanche told The Guardian that she has “a PhD and an MD degree,” and said she complies “with all mandatory FDA guidelines. Any publication to the contrary is false and defamatory.” She made note of her medical degree from a university in the British Caribbean territory of Montserrat and her previous work experience as a physician’s assistant, but added that she had never actually been a licensed physician in the U.S.
Yet those qualifications simply are not enough to be eligible for one of the government’s top public health positions, according to public health researchers.
“It absolutely concerns me,” Peter Lurie, the executive director of the Center for Science in the Public Interest, told The Guardian, reacting to Blanche’s appointment. “I have no confidence that the attorney general’s wife, with a financial interest in the kind of products this advisory committee concerns itself with, would be appropriate on the committee.”
Notably, the products to treat Epstein-Barr and HPV vanished from Blanche’s website the day after The Guardian sent her questions about them. Instead, the store now carries a disclaimer that “these statements have not been evaluated by the Food and Drug Administration. These products are not intended to diagnose, treat, cure, or prevent any disease.”
The president once attacked New York City’s traffic plan. Now, the federal government is making grants available for similar programs across the country.
Congestion Relief Zone signs on Park Avenue in New York City
Michael Nagle/Bloomberg/Getty Images
Congestion Relief Zone signs on Park Avenue in New York City
After years of trying to destroy New York City’s congestion pricing system, the Trump administration is now offering grants to take similar policies nationwide.
The Federal Highway Administration announced Thursday that it would invest $100 million to target and eliminate congestion, including funds to implement “HOV toll lanes, as well as congestion, cordon and parking pricing programs,” Gothamist reported.
Just hours after the announcement was made, that specific language was removed from the official online press release, according to Streetsblog NYC. Similar language describing congestion pricing can still be found in the description of the federal Congestion Relief Program.
Trump first announced that he would challenge New York City’s new congestion pricing program in February 2025 by declaring himself king. In March, a federal judge ruled that the Trump administration did not have the authority to revoke the city’s pricing policy. The Department of Transportation appealed that decision in June, arguing that it was the judge who had overstepped the bounds of their authority, and that the FHWA officials could revoke policies whenever it pleased them. The appeals court has yet to rule on the matter.
In August 2026, Trump again mocked congestion pricing, claiming that the program was being run by “Radical Left Jihadists,” referring to New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who was elected after the policy was already in place.
In a statement to Gothamist, DOT spokesperson Danna Almeida denied that the grants would possibly fund congestion pricing programs like the one in Manhattan.
“As the statute is written, the grant program is nothing like New York City’s illegal cordon pricing program, nor does it impact the ongoing litigation,” Almeida said. “The Secretary has been clear, dollars collected from tolling should be reinvested back into roads and drivers should have access to free alternative routes.”
Since the city first began charging drivers $9 during peak periods to drive south of 60th Street in Manhattan, New York’s Metropolitan Transportation Authority reports that traffic is down 15 percent.
Thought that President Donald Trump’s so-called “Anti-Weaponization” slush fund was dead? Not quite.
Trump administration officials intervened to secure a $2.5 million payout for five plaintiffs in a class-action lawsuit against the IRS, with each plaintiff getting half a million, ProPublica reported Thursday.
The Department of Justice initially sought to dismiss the case, but in August it intervened before the final fact-finding period with a proposal that would pay 250 times the legal limit of $1,000 for such cases.
The five plaintiffs included Shelby Lowman, a golf pro at Trump National Golf Club Hudson Valley, as well as Safe Harbor, a company connected to the president’s media business without a website or public presence. These plaintiffs alleged that the IRS and government contractor Booz Allen Hamilton had failed to securely safeguard their financial information—the same charges that Trump had levied against the IRS in his own $10 million lawsuit.
That lawsuit had resulted in the creation of the president’s $1.776 billion slush fund, paving the way for government payouts to anyone the administration saw fit. The fund was supposed to have been killed by court order months ago.
After these latest settlements, two more people connected to Trump businesses came forward to continue the litigation. Critics are concerned that even more plaintiffs could join in a backdoor attempt for Trump allies to receive massive payouts from the government.

sources.news_title: Katie Zacharia rejects California State Bar probe: "Politically motivated"
sources.text:
The California State Bar said Thursday that it had launched an investigation into claims made by President Donald Trump's former White House press secretary Katie Zacharia that she was an attorney.
In a letter sent to the Campaign for Accountability (CFA) which filed a complaint October 14, the Bar said it had forwarded the filing for further investigation.
Zacharia, who served as White House press secretary for less than a week in October, had said she was an attorney while living in California, after obtaining a law degree in 2011, but she was reported to have never been admitted to practice law in the state or elsewhere in the U.S.
Read More on Politics
"Zacharia may have thought she was just playing a lawyer on TV, but by repeatedly holding herself out as an attorney on news programs, she was pretending to have authority she lacks," CFA executive director Michelle Kuppersmith said in a press release. "We're pleased the California Bar is taking this matter seriously and investigating."
When reached for comment, a spokesperson for Zacharia called them "baseless allegations."
"This complaint is politically motivated and a clear waste of the State Bar’s time and resources," they told Newsweek. "We are confident it will be dismissed with no finding of wrongdoing."
The spokesperson said they had concerns about the state bar's letter being made public, adding that it was meant to be a private matter.
When Was Katie Zacharia Appointed?
Zacharia was announced as press secretary October 9, and she took over the role October 12. After holding just one short press briefing, she left the White House on October 16, making hers the shortest tenure in modern history.
She had replaced Karoline Leavitt, who worked on Trump's 2024 reelection campaign before becoming press secretary in January 2025. After a brief time away for maternity leave, Leavitt returned to the briefing room for a few months, before announcing her departure to spend more time with her two children.
Did Katie Zacharia Pass the Bar Exam? Rumors Explained
When Trump announced Zacharia's appointment last month, he referred to her as a lawyer, and she referred to herself as an attorney when appearing on television.
While she did sit for the California bar after obtaining her law degree from Pepperdine University in 2011, The Wall Street Journal reported October 14 that she had not passed the exam.
A day earlier, after appearing for her only briefing, Zacharia was asked in which state she had passed the bar. She responded, "When I moved to China."
When asked if he was upset that Zacharia had not disclosed that she did not pass the bar exam, Trump told reporters that week, "Well, I wasn’t hiring her to be a lawyer.
"I would say it probably wouldn’t have mattered. She’s been loyal to me since day one for a long time, but it’s not an easy job," Trump said.
The CFA then filed its complaint with the California State Bar, arguing the investigation was necessary.
According to Section 6126(a) of the California Business and Professions Code, it is a misdemeanor for anyone who is not an active licensee of the State Bar to hold themselves out as practicing or entitled to practice law. If found guilty, a person could face up to one year in jail and a $1,000 fine.
“The rules against unlicensed lawyering exist to protect the public," Kuppersmith said in an October press release. "To be meaningful, the rules must apply to people with the biggest megaphones, not just to those with no platform.”
The State Bar of California told Newsweek that it was aware of reports of an investigation regarding "non-licensee Katie Zacharia."
"The State Bar notes that neither the submission of a complaint nor the conduct of an investigation constitutes a finding that a non-licensee has engaged in unauthorized practice of law in violation of California statutes," a spokesperson said.
Newsweek’s reporters and editors used Martyn, our AI assistant, to produce this story. Learn more about Martyn here. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Samantha Beech and Edward T. Cummins

Katie Zacharia under investigation over legal work in California, state bar says
Trump’s ex-White House press secretary, who lasted only five days in the role, is accused of practicing law without a license
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Already a member? Log in
The State Bar of California has opened an investigation into former White House press secretary Katie Zacharia, who is accused of practicing law in the state without a license.
Zacharia, who lasted only five days as Donald Trump’s chief spokesperson, had previously claimed that she served as general counsel for a nonprofit organization in the state despite never passing the bar exam there or having any legal credentials to practice law anywhere in the U.S., let alone California.
After Trump tapped Zacharia as White House press secretary, several legal advocacy groups filed complaints with California’s bar following media reports that detailed her lack of legal experience.
In its letter to nonpartisan nonprofit group Campaign for Accountability, the state bar indicated that an investigation is underway, and the group’s complaint has been forwarded to an investigator and legal advisor.
“Zacharia may have thought she was just playing a lawyer on TV, but by repeatedly holding herself out as an attorney on news programs, she was pretending to have authority she lacks,” Campaign for Accountability executive director Michelle Kuppersmith said in a statement Thursday.
“These are baseless allegations,” a spokesperson for Zacharia told The Independent.
“This complaint is politically motivated and a clear waste of the State Bar’s time and resources,” the person added. “We are confident it will be dismissed with no finding of wrongdoing.”
Zacharia had repeatedly referred to herself as a lawyer throughout her media career, and Trump hailed Zacharia as an “attorney” in his Truth Social post announcing her appointment to the highly-scrutinized role.
After graduating from Pepperdine University’s Caruso School of Law in 2011, Zacharia worked for Chinese firm Zhong Lun, where she has claimed to have worked as an “outside counsel” to the World Bank and the International Finance Corporation. “It was an interesting and exciting experience,” she told The Buck Sexton Show last year.
From January 2024 to March 2025, she served as general counsel with Fix California, a right-wing nonprofit group founded by Richard Grenell, who previously served as acting director of national intelligence during the first Trump administration.
Fix California is “committed to pursuing long-term solutions that advance conservative ideas and causes throughout the state,” according to its website.
The group reported $557,089 in revenue in 2024, according to tax filings. It does not appear Zacharia was paid a salary, but she received $27,367 for her “in person and fundraising solicitation,” filings show.
The State Bar of California operates under the Supreme Court of California as the chief licensing organization for attorneys in the state. Zacharia’s name is not listed with the California bar, nor does she appear on the state’s list of attorneys under her maiden name.
Following media scrutiny into her legal credentials, Zacharia’s LinkedIn profile appears to have been updated to change her role with Fix California to “senior advisor.”
Zacharia’s profile also states that she was an “associate” on the “international practice team” at Zhong Lun Law Firm. The international firm has more than 400 partners and “2,200 professionals” in “17 locations throughout major financial centers in China as well as Hong Kong, Tokyo and New York,” according to its website.
“I practiced international transaction law, with all the appropriate credentials,” Zacharia said in a statement to The Independent last month.
Following her work with Zhong Lun and Fix California, Zacharia does not appear to have engaged in any other legal work. She began working as a commentator for right-wing media outlet Newsmax in 2024 and then as a commentator with Fox News the following year.
She also worked as a deputy assistant secretary for public affairs with the Department of Homeland Security from February to March of this year.
Since June, she has served as a senior communications adviser with the president’s social media platform Truth Social and its parent company Trump Media & Technology group before Trump brought her over to the White House.
Under California rules prohibiting the unauthorized practice of law, anyone found guilty of the misdemeanor of practicing law or falsely holding themselves out as a lawyer can face up to one year in a county jail and a fine of up to $1,000.
“The White House press secretary is the voice of the administration, we should be able to trust what he or she says,” Norm Eisen, a former White House ethics lawyer and co-founder of Democracy Defenders Fund, among groups that filed a complaint with the State Bar of California.
“How can we trust someone who appears to have held themselves out to be one thing when they are not?” he added. “No one is above the law, which is why we’re calling on the state bar and the attorney general to thoroughly investigate these serious allegations.”

“Zacharia may have thought she was just playing a lawyer on TV, but by repeatedly holding herself out as an attorney on news programs, she was pretending to have authority she lacks,” said Michelle Kuppersmith, the director of the Campaign for Accountability.
An official probe has been initiated against former White House press secretary Katie Zacharia by the State Bar of California following accusations from a watchdog organization that she continually claimed to be an attorney even though she never passed a bar exam.
The inquiry stems from an October 14 complaint filed by the Campaign for Accountability, which pointed to television appearances and online profiles where Zacharia claimed legal credentials.
In early November, the state bar notified the non-profit that it had assigned an investigator and legal adviser to examine the allegations, according to The Washington Post. Serving as the primary licensing body for attorneys within the jurisdiction, the State Bar of California functions under the authority of the Supreme Court of California.
Zacharia earned a law degree from Pepperdine University in Southern California in 2011, after completing an undergraduate degree there in 2007. Before her brief stint as White House press secretary, she appeared frequently on cable news networks such as Fox News and Newsmax as a legal and political commentator, with the complaint highlighting at least 18 appearances on Fox News alone starting in March 2025.
Her professional profile also listed her as general counsel for Fix California, a right-wing nonprofit organization founded by Trump ally Ric Grenell, where filings indicate she received $27,367 for fundraising and in-person solicitation.
When Donald Trump announced her appointment on October 9, he introduced her as an attorney. She officially took over the role on October 12 after replacing Karoline Leavitt. But questions quickly mounted regarding her background, leading to her departure from the White House on October 16 after serving for just five days, making hers the shortest tenure in modern history.
Her exit followed a rocky first press briefing where she struggled with her words and took questions predominantly from conservative media outlets. When reporters asked Trump that week if he was upset she had not disclosed failing the bar exam, he said that he was not hiring her to be a lawyer and that it probably would not have mattered.
Zacharia previously defended her terminology by pointing to a distinction between the terms “lawyer” and “attorney,” telling reporters and media outlets that holding a law degree allowed her to provide legal analysis rather than legal advice. She also referred reporters to an American Bar Association Journal article discussing the difference between the two titles. Legal experts consulted during the scrutiny noted a distinct gap between holding a law degree and holding a license to practice.
“Someone in the U.S. who just flat-out calls themselves a lawyer, without further qualification or explanation, will mislead listeners or readers to think that they are permitted to practice law here in the U.S.,” said Bruce Green, the director of the Louis Stein Center for Law and Ethics at Fordham University School of Law, as reported by The Daily Beast.
Under California Business and Professions Code Section 6125, practicing law or holding oneself out as entitled to practice without an active state bar license is a misdemeanor, and the watchdog’s complaint asks the state bar to determine whether she violated these statutes and to refer any potential violations to the Ventura County District Attorney or another appropriate prosecutor.
If found guilty, an individual can face up to one year in county jail and a fine of up to $1,000, according to International Business Times UK.
Zacharia’s representatives have firmly rejected the inquiry. “These are baseless allegations. This complaint is politically motivated and a clear waste of the state bar’s time and resources. We are confident it will be dismissed with no finding of wrongdoing,” a spokesperson for Zacharia said in a statement to The Guardian, expressing concern that the state bar’s notification letter was made public.
The State Bar of California, the largest in the United States with over 286,000 living members as of December 2022, was legally established on July 29, 1927, when the State Bar Act went into effect. It operates as an administrative division of the Supreme Court of California, responsible for licensing attorneys, regulating the practice of law, and investigating complaints of professional misconduct.
In 2018–2019, the State Bar was restructured into a standalone government entity focused on legal enforcement via the State Bar Court, separating from the voluntary California Lawyers Association. Membership in the State Bar remains mandatory for most practicing lawyers in California, and it acts as the administrative arm of the California Supreme Court in admission and discipline matters.
The State Bar of California has emphasized that launching an investigation does not constitute a formal finding of rule violations, and a spokesperson said that agency investigations remain confidential. The assigned investigator and legal adviser will review the submitted materials to determine whether further disciplinary or legal referrals are warranted.
